title: What to say
hookLine: a blank text box after a death, and five marks of well-spoken words
tomorrow: why would anyone chant to someone too sick to answer?

cards: A friend's message says someone they love has died. The reply box sits there, blinking. People type and delete.
Some send a heart and nothing else, then worry about it for a week. Everything sounds wrong: too much, too little, too much like a card. So when you do have to speak, what do you say?
The suttas have a short list for exactly this kind of moment, though it was never written only for funerals.

teach.b: In one sutta the Buddha names five marks of well-spoken words. They're spoken at the right time. They're true.
They're gentle. They're helpful. And they're spoken with a mind of goodwill.

Notice what isn't on the list: clever, complete, or long. In another sutta, the Buddha says of his own speech that he says only what is true and helpful, and he waits for the right time to say even a hard thing.
So the words that fit a loss tend to be small. Not: at least she isn't suffering. Not: I know exactly how you feel.
Those can sound wise and still land wrong. I'm so sorry. I'm here.
I loved her laugh. True, gentle, on time. And timing matters: a true thing said too soon can still land hard.
Silence is allowed too, the kind that stays in the room. That's the week, and it holds together. A mother walked a whole street and found no house untouched.
A queen's questions showed that grief is love. Even Ananda wept, and his teacher sent for him.
A warm mug showed that grief can be held gently. A gift given in someone's name is for them. And a basin of water said: just be there.
When words are needed, simple words.

how: Buddhists practice right speech as part of the eightfold path; at a death, condolences in Buddhist communities are often brief, with a bow, joined palms or a few quiet words to the family.

o: a set prayer every Buddhist must recite at a funeral
a few true, gentle words at the right time, or a kind silence
a polite way to change the subject away from the death

games.q: the five marks of well-spoken words — tap the pairs.

s: the best condolence is a long, wise message
the five marks are timely, true, gentle, helpful and kind. long and clever aren't on the list.
the sutta's marks of good speech include being spoken at the right time
timing is the first of the five.
saying nothing at all is always a failure of kindness
a silence that stays in the room can be the kindest thing on hand.

games.q: at the funeral, your friend's aunt asks you how her nephew is doing. honestly, he's a mess. what fits the five marks?
o: tell her he's doing great, so she won't worry today.
say gently that he's hurting, and that you're staying close to him.
list everything that's gone wrong for him this month, so she knows.
games.why: true and gentle, at the right time, with goodwill. no comforting lie, no flood of detail.

practice: Think of one person who's carrying something heavy right now. In your head or on your phone, shape one short sentence for them that is true, gentle and kind, and nothing more.
Read it back slowly, and take out any word that's trying too hard, any advice, any silver lining; what's left is usually enough. Keep it ready to send when the time is right.

wordCard.voice: What to say: words at the right time, true, gentle, helpful and kind, from a mind of goodwill. Small is fine. Silence that stays in the room is fine too.

orig.note: Pali samma vaca: right speech, a step of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Keep this: simple words, because I'm sorry, I'm here, is a whole sentence. Twenty days of thirty, and a week of grief, walked through.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.198, Vaca Sutta (five factors of well-spoken speech: timely, true, gentle, beneficial, with a mind of goodwill)
Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the Buddha speaks what is true and beneficial, knowing the right time)
